name: Chipewyan
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Chipewyan (chip1261) is not in the catalog. The sweep's only target item, Leer 1976 'Spirantization and the Development of Suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan' (Glottolog 167470 = ANLA CA965L1976b), was located as an open scan on the ANLA server (the ANLA record page loads via https://uafanlc.alaska.edu/drupal/api/record and the file list via search.php?res=; the host has an incomplete certificate chain, fetched sources with -k), downloaded (86 scanned pages, no text layer) and scanned at 200 dpi one tesseract at a time. It is a comparative tonogenesis manuscript (PA constriction/glottalization -> tone in daughter stems); Chipewyan appears only as a tone-reflex language ('in Chipewyan the reflex is high tone with the loss of the final glottal stop', scan p. 18) and the words 'stress'/'accent' do not occur anywhere in the scanned. Relevance: prosody-but-not-word-stress; priority none. From material already on file, the best first-hand word-stress statement is Jaker & Howson 2022 (Phonology 39, CC-BY) p. 11: Tetsǫ́t’ıné (a dialect of Dëne Sųłıné) has quantity-sensitive, left-to-right, iterative iambic stress with high tone attracting stress and rightmost stress primary (p. 18); Goddard 1912 pp. 82-83 gives an older, self-described incomplete Cold Lake statement (stress on the semantically important/stem syllable). All

earlier_scan.source_named: Cook, Eung-Do. 2004. A Grammar of Dene Suline (Chipewyan). Winnipeg: Algonquian and Iroquoian Linguistics; also Li Fang-Kuei 1946 'Chipewyan' in Linguistic Structures of Native America. Wikipedia phonology section covers tone only, no stress.

new_statements.quote: Tetsǫ́t’ıné is a quantity-sensitive, left-to-right iambic system in which high tone attracts stress. If we put aside the role of tone, the interaction between quantity and iambic feet in Tetsǫ́t’ıné is typologically normal for an iambic system (cf. Hayes 1995). Thus, every heavy syllable constitutes the head of a foot. Light syllables can form a foot together with a heavy syllable to their immediate right, or else two light syllables can also form a foot. [...] Note also that we assume that word-final light syllables are extrametrical [p. 11]. [...] We propose that Tetsǫ́t’ıné stress is iambic by default. Because high tone attracts stress, in accordance with the TSP (DeLacy 2002, 2007), however, a high–low tone pattern will result in a trochee in two-syllable words [p. 17].
new_statements.citation: Jaker, Alessandro & Phil J. Howson. 2022. An acoustic study of Tetsǫ́t’ıné stress: Iambic stress in a quantity-sensitive tone language. Phonology 39(1): 1–39. doi:10.1017/S0952675722000069
new_statements.locator: §3.4, p. 11 (first quote); §4, p. 17 (second quote); secondary stress §4, p. 18
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (39 pp., Cambridge Core CC-BY download; PDF page numbers = printed page numbers). Quote 1 is verbatim on p. 11 (section 3.4 'Distributional evidence for stress', second paragraph: 'Tetsǫ́t’ıné is a quantity-sensitive, left-to-right iambic system in which high tone attracts stress. If we put aside the role of tone... every heavy syllable constitutes the head of a foot. Light syllables can form a foot together with a heavy syllable to their immediate right, or else two light syllables can also form a foot.' and 'Note also that we assume that word-final light syllables are extrametrical, as in (13e).'); the reader's '[...]' and '[p. 11]' are its own elisions/markers, the wording itself…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Left-to-right, quantity-sensitive iambic feet: every heavy (long-vowel or word-final closed) syllable is a foot head; a light syllable groups with a following heavy or light syllable to form a (L ˈH)/(L ˈL) iamb; feet are iterative so words carry more than one stress, and the rightmost stress is (impressionistically) primary. High tone attracts stress, so H–L sequences surface as trochees and a low-toned syllable after a high-toned one is unstressed; final light syllables are extrametrical. Duration is the main acoustic cue, intensity secondary, F0 not a cue (tone is contrastive).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Iterative footing gives more than one stress per prosodic word (e.g. (ˈheː)(ˈtãː) 'they drink', (ja.ˈneɬ)(ˈthiː) 'you speak'); 'Jaker's subjective impression is that where there is more than one stress in a prosodic word, the rightmost stress is the primary stress' (p. 18); the acoustic study found no significant duration or intensity difference between primary and secondary stress (fn. 4, p. 18).
new_statements.exceptions: High tone attracts stress: a high–low tone pattern yields a trochee in disyllables (e.g. (ˈhí.tãː) 'we drink'); a low-toned syllable following a high-toned one is unstressed (final syllable unstressed in L-H-L and H-H-L words, e.g. (he.ˈné)kheː); word-final light syllables are extrametrical ((ˈthaː)ɣe 'three'); coda consonants in prefixes are generally non-moraic except in 1PL hít and 2PL uh, while word-final codas are moraic. Older Cold Lake description (Goddard 1912: 82) instead places accent on the semantically most important syllable (the stem in verbs) with some words always final-stressed and many words with two accents, and calls itself 'quite incomplete'.
new_statements.domain_note: Prosodic word; verbs only in the acoustic study (all stems obligatorily heavy and word-final); citation-form verb paradigms elicited from four Tetsǫ́t’ıné speakers in Yellowknife and Łutselk’e. Ordinary (non-neutralising) case: stress position adjusts to fixed tone and vowel length; a minority of cases show tone shift, vowel-length transfer and consonant deletion driven by iambic footing (§3.4).
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement describes Tetsǫ́t’ıné, the Yellowknives Dene dialect of Dëne Sųłıné spoken at Dettah/N'dilo and Łutselk'e, NWT (ISO chp; Jaker & Howson 2022 p. 4: 'a dialect of Dëne Sųłıné'). Glottolog 5.1 lists three chip1261 dialects — Eastern Chipewyan east2857, Western Chipewyan west2954, Old Yellowknife Chipewyan oldy1234 — the last being the historical Yellowknife variety; the modern Tetsǫ́t’ıné has no separate glottocode, so the entry should be filed under chip1261 with the dialect flagged. The older Cold Lake (Alberta) dialect statement of Goddard 1912: 82 (semantic/stem-based accent, some final-stress words, two accents per word) is impressionistic and self-described as incomplete; Cook 2004 (Cold Lake-based grammar) was not accessible and may give a different language-level statement.

new_statements.quote: Tetsǫ́t’ıné is a quantity-sensitive, left-to-right iambic system in which high tone attracts stress. If we put aside the role of tone, the interaction between quantity and iambic feet in Tetsǫ́t’ıné is typologically normal for an iambic system (cf. Hayes 1995). Thus, every heavy syllable constitutes the head of a foot. Light syllables can form a foot together with a heavy syllable to their immediate right, or else two light syllables can also form a foot.
new_statements.citation: Jaker, Alessandro & Phil J. Howson (2022). An acoustic study of Tetsǫ́t’ıné stress: Iambic stress in a quantity-sensitive tone language. Phonology 39(1): 1-39. doi:10.1017/S0952675722000069
new_statements.locator: p. 11, §3.4 'Distributional evidence for stress' (variety identified p. 5: Tetsǫ́t’ıné is a dialect of Dëne Sųłıné, Ethnologue CHP); secondary stress p. 18
new_statements.reading: Word stress in the Tetsǫ́t’ıné (Yellowknives) dialect of Dëne Sųłıné/Chipewyan is quantity-sensitive iambic, parsed left to right and iterative: every heavy (long-vowel) syllable is stressed, light syllables pair with a following heavy or with another light syllable in (L H)/(L L) iambs, high tone attracts stress, and the rightmost stress is primary; stress coexists with four tones and phonemic vowel length. For a catalog coding this is 'iambic, quantity-sensitive, left-to-right, multiple stress' at the dialect level (Tetsǫ́t’ıné), with the older Cold Lake description (Goddard 1912 p. 82: stress on the semantically important/stem syllable, incomplete) as the only other first-hand statement read.

If we put aside the role of tone, the interaction between quantity and iambic feet in Tetsǫ́t’ıné is typologically normal for an iambic system (cf. Hayes 1995). sources.locator: §3.4, p. 11 (first quote); §4, p. 17 (second quote); secondary stress §4, p. 18
sources.note: Tetsǫ́t’ıné (Yellowknives dialect of Dëne Sųłıné) has a quantity-sensitive, left-to-right iambic stress system in which high tone attracts stress (p. 11); stress is iterative, word-final light syllables extrametrical, every heavy syllable heads a foot; H–L tone pattern yields a trochee in disyllables (p. 17); rightmost stress is primary (Jaker's impression, p. 18); acoustically duration is the primary correlate, intensity secondary, no F0 effect (pp. 23–36).

sources.citation: Goddard, Pliny Earle (1912). Analysis of Cold Lake Dialect, Chipewyan. Anthropological Papers of the AMNH 10(2): 67-170. [Not in the target list; already on file; read here.]
sources.quote: p. 82: 'Something resembling the stress accent of English is heard with considerable regularity in Chipewyan. As has been said in the preceding section it rests on the syllable having the greater importance as to the meaning of the word. ... A few words like e na', Cree (Fig. 73) and dün ni', moose (Fig. 88) are always accented on the final syllable. The latter word may be a verb form with the stem -ni "to make a noise" and have the accent on the stem as is usual in verbs. Many words have two accents ...' p. 83: 'The above statement is quite incomplete for the subject of stress is difficult in any case ...'
sources.note: Early kymographic description of Cold Lake Chipewyan: stress falls on the semantically most important syllable (the stem in verbs; e.g. dlo'ne 'mouse' initial, dün ni' 'moose' final), many words carry two accents; the author calls his statement incomplete. Consistent with a morphologically anchored (stem) stress rather than a fixed edge position.

sources.citation: Leer, Jeff (1976). Spirantization and the Development of Suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan. Ms. dated 7-21-76, 24 pp. + typescript 30 pp. Alaska Native Language Archive item CA965L1976b (Glottolog ref 167470, hhtype comparative).
sources.quote: One of the major purposes of this paper is to formulate a hypothesis of the development of tone in modern Athabaskan from an earlier (pre-Proto-Athabaskan) system of vowel nuclei ... [scan p. 18:] In most cases the tone reflex of syllables with final glottal stop agrees with that of the constricted vowels: in Navajo, Sarcee, and Kutchin the reflex is generally low tone, whereas in Chipewyan the reflex is high tone with the loss of the final glottal stop.
sources.locator: scan p. 18 (typescript section B; no printed page numbers survive scanned); scan pp. 2-4 introduction
sources.note: Nothing. The manuscript is a comparative-historical study of tonogenesis (Proto-Athabaskan constriction/glottalization of stem vowels and stem-final consonants -> high vs low tone in the daughter languages); Chipewyan appears only as one of thirteen reflex languages for tone. The scan (86 pages: handwritten draft + typescript) has no text layer; after scanned at 200 dpi the words 'stress' and 'accent' occur nowhere in the text. Not a source for word-stress placement in Chipewyan.

sources.citation: Goddard, Pliny Earle. 1912. Texts and analysis of Cold Lake dialect, Chipewyan. Anthropological Papers of the American Museum of Natural History 10(1–2): 1–170 (Analysis pp. 67–170)
sources.note: 'Stress' section p. 82: something like English stress accent is heard regularly; it rests on the syllable of greatest semantic importance (the stem, 'as is usual in verbs'); a few words (ena' 'Cree', dunni' 'moose') always final-stressed; many words carry two accents; author calls the statement 'quite incomplete'. 'Pitch' p. 83: pitch differences noted (after Legoff), no contour tone within the syllable; final syllable usually slightly lowered.

sources.quote: 'Dans l’espèce, ce n’est, en effet, ni plus ni moins, que l’accent donné à ces consonnes et le ton accompagnant la pronunciation qui déterminent leur signification.' [In this case it is, in effect, neither more nor less than the accent given to these consonants and the tone accompanying the pronunciation that determine their meaning.]
sources.note: Only a remark that 'accent' and tone distinguish meanings; no rule for where word stress falls.
